content: Mission Zamora is a comprehensive land reform and redistribution initiative in Venezuela, established through the Ley de Tierras (Law of the Land), one of 49 decrees issued by President Hugo Chávez in November 2001. The program is named after Ezequiel Zamora, a 19th-century Venezuelan peasant leader. Venezuela's rural areas have experienced significant economic neglect, depopulation, and abandonment since the discovery of oil wealth in the early 20th century. This has led to an urbanization rate exceeding 85%, one of the highest in Latin America. Despite possessing vast tracts of fertile and arable land, Venezuela has become a net importer of food. The Ley de Tierras was enacted to address these issues by implementing land reforms, including redistribution, under the framework of Plan Zamora. The objectives of Plan Zamora include revitalizing Venezuela's agricultural sector to ensure food security, reducing the country's reliance on food imports, and stimulating economic activity. The program also aims to dismantle the concentrated economic power of the latifundios (large estates), where 75-80% of the land is owned by just 5% of landowners, and 60% of farmers own no land at all. Additionally, the plan seeks to redistribute wealth to the poor and curb urbanization, which places immense strain on city services, particularly in the slums of Caracas and other urban centers. Underutilized or unused private corporate and agricultural estates are now subject to expropriation, with fair-market compensation provided to the owners. Small farmers and farming collectives are granted inheritable, inalienable, and sometimes communal land grants. The rationale for this program is to incentivize the gradual repopulation of rural areas and to enhance the country's food security by reducing dependence on foreign imports. Three categories of land are eligible for redistribution under the program: 1. Government-owned land. 2. Land claimed by private owners but disputed by the government, including land inherited over centuries. 3. Underutilized private land, such as second homes and investment properties. To date, the Chávez government has only redistributed the first two types of land. The legal framework of Plan Zamora includes three key components: 1. A capped limit on the size of landholdings, varying between 1 and 50 km² depending on conditions. 2. A tax on unused landholdings. 3. A program for the redistribution of government-owned and expropriated unused private lands, with compensation. Venezuelan citizens aged 18 to 25, or those heading a family, may petition to benefit from the land redistribution programs. Participants are initially granted a piece of land to homestead and cultivate. If they cultivate the land continuously for three years, they are awarded official title to the land. This government-recognized title can be inherited by the participants' relatives but cannot be sold. Three institutions were established to implement the land distribution program: 1. The Instituto Nacional de Tierras (National Land Institute), which oversees land tenancy. 2. The Instituto Nacional de Desarrollo Rural (National Rural Development Institute), which provides aid to farmers, including technical expertise and equipment. 3. The Corporación de Abastecimiento y Servicios Agrícolas (Agricultural Corporation of Supplies and Services), which assists with marketing. By the end of 2003, 60,000 families had received temporary titles to a total of 55,000 km² of land under this plan. The program faced significant opposition. The Venezuelan Federation of Chambers of Commerce (Fedecámaras) and the Venezuelan Labor Federation (CTV) organized a general strike on December 10, 2001, a month after the 49 decrees were passed. During the April 2002 coup attempt, Fedecámaras leader Pedro Carmona, who briefly assumed the presidency, reversed the 49 decrees, including the Ley de Tierras. However, this reversal was declared null when the coup failed, and Chávez returned to power.
